SK2164 The assertion's expression has side effects

An argument of a call to a [Conditional]-attributed method — Debug.Assert and Trace.Assert above all — assigns, increments, awaits or mutates a framework collection, so the effect happens only in the builds where the call survives.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS3346

Why

[Conditional("DEBUG")] does not make the condition true in release; it deletes the call site, arguments and all. Debug.Assert(pending.Remove(id)) therefore removes the entry in every debug run and in no release run. The bug exists only in production, vanishes under a debugger, and survives the test suite intact — because the suite is a debug build, so the effect is there and the assertion passes. It is the rare defect that running the code more carefully makes less visible.

Example

Instead of:

Debug.Assert(pending.Remove(id));

Write:

var removed = pending.Remove(id);
Debug.Assert(removed);

When it does not fire

⚠ The rule is on `[Conditional]`, not on a list of assertion methods, and the generalisation costs nothing. Debug.Assert and Trace.Assert are the motivating case and by far the commonest, but the defect is a property of the attribute: a repository's own [Conditional("TRACE")] logging helper deletes its arguments in exactly the same way, and a rule naming only the framework's two would be silent on the version somebody wrote themselves. The attribute is looked for on the method and on every method it overrides. The whole analyzer withdraws when System.Diagnostics.ConditionalAttribute does not resolve.

⚠ An xUnit, NUnit or MSTest assertion is out of scope by construction, which is the answer to the shape that would otherwise be this rule's worst false positive. Assert.True(map.TryGetValue(key, out var found)) is idiomatic and correct: none of the three frameworks marks its assertions [Conditional], so the call is never deleted, the effect always happens, and there is nothing to report. The rule cannot reach that shape rather than reaching it and filtering it out — which also makes it disjoint from SK8007, whose subject is a test assertion consuming a live clock or an unseeded random value, a different question about a different set of calls.

⚠ What counts as a side effect is enumerated, never inferred. "Does this method mutate" is undecidable, and a rule that guessed would report Debug.Assert(list.Any()) and be switched off the same afternoon. Four kinds of evidence are accepted, each a fact about the syntax or about a framework symbol: an assignment in any spelling; an increment or decrement; an `await`, whose awaited work is what disappears rather than merely its result; and a call to a framework collection member whose contract is to mutate.

⚠ The collection namespaces are listed exactly, and `System.Collections.Immutable` is the reason. A prefix test on "System.Collections" reads naturally and is wrong: ImmutableList<T>.Add and ImmutableDictionary<K, V>.Remove return a new collection and mutate nothing, so every one of them would be a false positive. System.Collections.Frozen is excluded for the same reason. The member must also come from metadata, so a source type's Remove is never matched — the rule cannot know what it does.

⚠ An `out var` was built as a fifth kind of evidence and then removed, because the compiler already reports it — and the refutation came from a fixture that would not compile rather than from an argument. Where the variable is read below the assertion, deleting the call leaves it unassigned and the read is CS0165, use of unassigned local variable, in any build without the symbol defined; the harness's rule that a fixture which does not compile proves nothing is what surfaced it. docs/plan/08 § "the compiler already says it" then decides the question: a rule restating a compiler error adds a second voice and no information. Where the variable is not read, nothing is wrong at all — the value was never wanted. Both directions are now silence.

The walk descends into lambdas on purpose: the whole argument is deleted, so an effect written inside a lambda the argument hands to All or Any is deleted with it, and stopping at the lambda boundary would be silent on the shape most likely to hide one. Every argument is inspected, not only the condition, because the call site is deleted whole. At most one finding is emitted per call.

⚠ No fix. The two repairs are to hoist the effect into a local above the assertion and to delete the assertion, and choosing between them is the entire content of the finding — the question is whether the effect was meant to happen at all. The hoist additionally needs an identifier that does not exist yet, and inventing a name that cannot shadow a field, collide with a local or read as nonsense is not something an edit to one file's text can promise.
